props.title: Breaking Glass
props.initialSlug: Punk singer's rise and fall in corrupt music biz

sections.content: Breaking Glass epitomizes British punk's transition into the new wave era, following Hazel O'Connor's Kate as she navigates the music industry's dark underbelly. Like Jubilee (1978) and The Great Rock 'n' Roll Swindle (1980), it captures punk's raw energy while critiquing commercialization. The film's dystopian elements and neon-soaked visuals influenced later music films like Ladies and Gentlemen, the Fabulous Stains (1982) and Smithereens (1982).

sections.content: The film stands out for its prescient commentary on music video culture, predating MTV by a year. O'Connor's theatrical performances, particularly "Eighth Day" and "Will You," established a visual template that would influence artists like Annie Lennox and Siouxsie Sioux. Rude Boy (1980) with The Clash and Dance Craze (1981) similarly documented this pivotal moment when punk evolved into new wave and post-punk. SUBHEAD: British Music Film Renaissance

Breaking Glass emerged during a fertile period for British music films, alongside That'll Be The Day (1973) and Stardust (1974). These films shared a commitment to showing the industry's darker side, contrasting with Hollywood's more sanitized approach in films like The Buddy Holly Story (1978). The gritty realism and social commentary would influence later works like Control (2007) and 24 Hour Party People (2002).
